lesson.title: Equivalent Fractions: Same Amount, Different Names

steps.say: Imagine you and your friend each get a small pizza at a birthday party in Kelowna. Yours is cut into two big pieces, and you eat one of them. Your friend's pizza is cut into four smaller pieces, and they eat two of them. Who ate more? Look carefully — you both ate exactly the same amount of pizza! One half and two quarters are the same size, they just have different names.

visual.caption: Same amount of pizza, cut two different ways

steps.say: Fractions that name the same amount are called equivalent fractions. Equivalent just means equal in value. Here are the very same two fractions drawn as bars instead of pizzas. See how the shaded parts line up perfectly? That is your proof that one half equals two quarters.

visual.caption: The shaded parts are exactly the same length

steps.say: So how do we make one on purpose? Here is the little secret. Cutting each piece into more pieces does not change how much you have. If you cut every piece into two, you get twice as many pieces, and you have twice as many shaded. So we multiply the top number and the bottom number by the same number. The same number, both times — that is the whole rule.

Let's try one together. You have three quarters of a chocolate bar. Let's find another name for it. Multiply the top by two, three times two is six. Multiply the bottom by two, four times two is eight. So three quarters equals six eighths. Look at the bars — the same amount of chocolate, just cut into skinnier pieces.

Now something a bit trickier. Two thirds of a garden bed is planted with carrots. Can we write that in twelfths? Ask yourself, what times three gives twelve? Three times four is twelve, so our magic number is four. Now do the same thing on top: two times four is eight. So two thirds equals eight twelfths.

visual.caption: Both bottoms and tops multiplied by four

steps.say: The rule also works backwards, using division. Say you drank six tenths of a bottle of water. Both six and ten can be divided by two. Six divided by two is three, and ten divided by two is five. So six tenths is the same as three fifths. When we go this direction and make the numbers smaller, we say we are putting the fraction in simplest form.

visual.caption: Dividing top and bottom by two gives the same amount

steps.say: Here is one last way to see it. On a number line from zero to one, three quarters and six eighths do not sit near each other — they sit on the exact same dot. Equivalent fractions always land on the same spot, because they really are the same number wearing a different outfit.

visual.caption: Different names, same point on the line

lesson.answer: Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number, and the fraction gets a new name but stays the exact same amount.

practice.question: Sofia drank 4 tenths of a 1 litre carton of milk. Write that amount as a fraction in fifths.
practice.answer: 2 fifths. Divide the top and bottom by 2: four divided by two is two, ten divided by two is five, so four tenths equals two fifths (that is 400 millilitres).
